claims.statement: The page is for repository administrators. Merge queues on FPT/GHEC require organization-owned public repositories or organization-owned private repositories on Enterprise Cloud; user-owned private Pro repositories do not qualify under this pinned reusable. GHES allows organization-owned repositories.

A merge queue tests changes against the latest base and earlier queued pull requests after their ordinary required checks pass; it can use Actions or another CI provider. This is documented behavior, not measured local execution.

A classic protection branch pattern containing * cannot use merge queues. Required queue checks must be triggered and reported by the CI provider, and queue configuration is coupled to branch protection or rulesets.
Actions CI must include merge_group for queued PRs; the example also retains pull_request. A passing PR-event run alone does not cover the group revision.
Third-party CI must handle the temporary gh-readonly-queue/{base_branch} prefix; the queued group SHA differs from the pull-request SHA.
Administrators can select Require merge queue in classic protection and choose merge, rebase or squash. These are configuration choices, not adoption of any method.
Build concurrency is 1–100 and controls maximum dispatched merge_group webhooks. It is separate from the number of PRs in a merge group.

Only merge non-failing pull requests can require each PR to pass, or permit failing individual PRs when the final combined group passes. The latter is a source option, not a recommendation to weaken the local draft policy.
A configured status-check timeout treats a still-unknown result as failure. The source gives no universally adopted local timeout.

Minimum and maximum merge limits each range 1–100, and the minimum-wait timeout may allow fewer than the minimum. Merge limits do not combine builds: they govern merging after group checks succeed. Deployment examples do not select local thresholds.
Queue processing is first-in-first-out once requirements are satisfied; groups contain latest base plus earlier queued changes and merge only after base-branch protections pass.

The main/pr-1/pr-2 examples illustrate group ancestry, successful merging after checks, rejection on failed checks or conflicts, and rebuilding later PRs without rejected predecessors. They are not real canary receipts.
The included removal reasons are CI failure, check timeout, requested removal, or unresolved branch-protection failure; removal itself is not successful enforcement recovery evidence.
Jump to the top rebuilds all in-progress groups because commit ancestry changes; the feature may slow merging. The PR1/2/3 example is explanatory, not local queue authority.
Further-reading links are navigation; destination article bodies are not reviewed by this receipt.

scope: Full pinned article plus literal dependency reading; source evidence only, without adoption or live behavior verification.
